sections.heading: Taking my proper place before you
sections.text: Most High God, it is right for me to come low before you. You are God, and I am not. I am small compared with you, and I do not have the strength or glory of the angels. Still, you made me as I am and put me where I am. Help me receive my life from your hand without resentment, and teach me to trust your wise rule over me.
theological_themes: trust in God's sovereignty and providence

scripture_references.connection: Peter calls believers to humble themselves under God's mighty hand, trusting that God's timing and rule are better than self-exaltation or resistance.
Paul teaches that God appoints human lives, times, and places, and that every person depends on him for life itself. This grounds the prayer's acceptance of being made and placed by God.

sections.heading: Thanking you that I can grow by grace
sections.text: Thank you that my life now is not the whole story. I am at the beginning of an existence meant for you, and by your grace I can still be changed. You made me to bear your image, not as a lifeless object being pushed along, but as a person you call to know you, obey you, and join in what you are doing. Let my life serve your purposes and bring you honor.
theological_themes: participation in God's work and glory

scripture_references.connection: Human beings are created in God's image and given a vocation under him. This supports the prayer's gratitude that life has dignity, purpose, and responsibility before God.
Paul describes believers being transformed into the Lord's image by the Spirit. This fits the prayer's hope that grace can improve and reshape the person over time.
Salvation by grace leads to a life of good works prepared by God. The prayer's desire to work with God and advance his glory belongs within that gospel-shaped calling.

sections.heading: Confessing what sin has done in me
sections.text: But Father, I cannot pretend I am what I should be. The crown has fallen from my head. I have sinned against you. Left to myself, I am estranged from you. My heart is not trustworthy; my thinking bends away from your law and argues against you. I need mercy, not excuses.
theological_themes: alienation from God apart from grace

scripture_references.connection: Paul states that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, which matches the prayer's image of lost honor and moral ruin before God.
Jeremiah exposes the deep deceitfulness of the human heart. This supports the prayer's refusal to trust its own inner life as innocent or reliable.
Paul describes sinners as once alienated and hostile in mind, yet reconciled through Christ. This directly illumines the prayer's confession of estrangement and its movement toward mediation.

sections.heading: Resting in the Mediator you have given
sections.text: Yet in my lostness you did not leave me without help. You laid my help on the Mighty One. Jesus stands between you and me—not to keep me from you, but to bring me back to you. He is the true Mediator I needed. His blood gives me peace with you. His righteousness is my strength. His being condemned in my place sets me free. His Spirit gives me power to live. His inheritance is the future you are giving me.
theological_themes: Christ as mediator between God and sinners
freedom through Christ's condemnation in our place
the Spirit's power and the believer's inheritance

scripture_references.connection: Job longs for an arbiter who could lay a hand on both God and man. The prayer takes that longing and sees its answer in Christ, who truly mediates between God and sinners.

Paul explicitly identifies Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity, who gave himself as a ransom. This grounds the prayer's confidence that Christ comes between God and the sinner for reconciliation.

Paul connects freedom from condemnation with God condemning sin in Christ and with life by the Spirit. This supports the prayer's language of Christ's condemnation becoming the believer's freedom and the Spirit becoming the believer's power.

Paul teaches that Christ was made sin for us so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. This explains the prayer's confidence that Christ's righteousness, not personal merit, is the believer's strength.

sections.heading: Asking grace to change me and hold me
sections.text: Please let me feel the strength of your grace more deeply. Subdue the evil that still lives in me. Loosen my grip on this present world where it pulls me away from you. Hold me up when life is hard. Teach me to stay near you even in the low places. Train me to live with a clear conscience before you and before other people.

scripture_references.connection: God's grace not only forgives but trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live for Christ. This fits the prayer's request for grace that actively subdues sin and frees from the present evil world.
The Lord tells Paul that divine grace is sufficient and that power is made perfect in weakness. This supports the prayer's dependence on grace for endurance under life's trials.
Paul speaks of striving to keep a clear conscience before God and people. The prayer asks for the same integrity in both the vertical and horizontal dimensions of life.

sections.heading: Choosing duty over anxiety
sections.text: In everything I have to face, help me tell the difference between what you have actually given me to do and what my fear is trying to make me carry. Let me care most about the kind of person I am becoming before you, not mainly about how easy or hard my circumstances are. Make me faithful in my responsibilities and free from anxious self-rule.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus directs his disciples to seek God's kingdom and righteousness rather than being consumed by tomorrow's troubles. This supports the prayer's distinction between present duty and anxious burden.
Paul tells believers to bring anxieties to God in prayer, promising God's peace to guard them. This grounds the request to be freed from anxiety without abandoning real responsibilities.
Paul states plainly that God's will includes the believer's sanctification. This supports the prayer's desire that character before God matter more than outward circumstances.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly reflects Puritan/Augustinian convictions about human sinfulness, including alienation from God, a deceitful heart, and hostility to God's law. This was preserved rather than softened.

The line about God making and placing the person where they are, and the request to accept God's sovereign pleasure, could be misunderstood as passive acceptance of injustice or harmful circumstances. The adaptation frames it as trust in God's wise rule without implying that evil should never be resisted.

The phrase "whose condemnation is my freedom" is theologically dense and could sound as if Christ himself is morally condemned. It was rendered as Christ being condemned in the sinner's place, consistent with substitutionary atonement and Romans 8:1-4.
significant_interpretive_choices: "In the embryo state of my endless being" was interpreted as the present earthly life being the beginning stage of an eternal existence before God, not as speculation beyond the prayer's basic Christian hope.

The phrase "I can bear thy image, not by submissiveness, but by design" is difficult in the supplied text. I rendered it as purposeful, personal participation in God's design rather than passive or mechanical conformity.
"Umpire, Daysman, Mediator" was interpreted through Job's longing for an arbiter and the New Testament teaching that Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity.
"May my character and not my circumstances chiefly engage me" was rendered as caring most about holiness and faithfulness rather than being governed by outward ease or hardship.
